Beállítom Magyar Péter szerdán honvédségi helikopterrel ment a paksi atomerőműhöz , ott lesz a kormányülés is. A miniszterelnök a képhez azt írta, a „fontos kormányzati döntések előtt a vízügyi szakemberek és az erőmű vezetői fentről is bemutatják a kialakult helyzetet, és felvázolják a mérnökök által megtervezett hosszú távú megoldási lehetőséget”. Hadházy Ákos később két fotót osztott meg a „Keresd a különbséget a két képen!” kezdetű posztjában, az egyiken a helikopterező Magyar Péter, a másikon a helikopterező Orbán Viktor látható. A politikus szerint az út egy helikopterrel is 1,5-2 millióba kerülhetett, és nem tudja elképzelni, hogy milyen szakmai döntést befolyásolhatott. Amennyiben semmilyet, akkor „ez a több milliós kiadás csak propaganda célokat szolgál” – írta. A posztról író HVG cikke alatt megjelent a miniszterelnök: „Természetesen van különbség, nem is kicsi” kezdetű kommentjében azt írta, hogy Hadházy is hamarosan látni fogja a megjelenő kormánydöntéseket és csütörtök reggeltől a munka megkezdését is. „Lehet, hogy ön egy asztal mellett döntene miniszterelnökként az ország sorsát nagyban befolyásoló kérdésekben, én viszont jobbnak látom, ha a szakemberek megmutatják minden oldalról az összes lehetséges opciót” – magyarázta a helikopterezést, hozzátéve, hogy a helikopternek és a pilótának is meg van szabva az éves minimum repülési ideje, amit sajnos így is nehezen érnek el, így a repülés költsége amúgy is felmerült volna. https://www.dw.com/en/iran-bets-on-shado.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5KtwR Iran is seeking new ways to bypass increasingly stringent US sanctions [FILE: February 23, 2016] Image: Ahmad Halabisaz/Xinhua/IMAGO Advertisement With its toughest sanctions yet , the administration of US President Donald Trump is seeking to force Iran's leadership into submission. The measures, dubbed "economic D-Day" sanctions , are intended to achieve what military pressure since February has failed to accomplish . In addition to targeting Iran's key sources of revenue and trade, including oil, banking, gold, shipping, aviation and certain technology sectors, US authorities are increasingly focusing on cryptocurrencies . Digital currencies such as bitcoin , which operate outside the traditional banking system and dollar-based financial networks, are being used by Iran for money transfers, trade transactions and, increasingly, oil-related business. An opaque network to help Tehran bypass sanctions Iran also appears to be exploring cryptocurrencies as a way to secure oil shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz . According to the Fars News Agency, which is close to Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the idea was proposed by Babak Zanjani. The 53-year-old billionaire was released from prison last year and remains one of the most prominent figures in a network that has grown over decades and helped Iran navigate international sanctions. In 2016, Zanjani became entangled in Iran's internal power struggles and was sentenced to death Image: Tasnim News/AFP Individuals within these networks enjoy support and protection from influential figures inside the Islamic Republic. In return, they are believed to share part of their profits with powerful patrons within the system. "Among these people, Zanjani belongs to an economic elite with innovative ideas and has repeatedly demonstrated his capabilities in the past," said Behzad Ahmadinia, an Iran-born journalist based in Cyprus who specializes in the oil and energy sector. "It appears that the regime has decided to overcome internal rivalries and rely on professionals and experts who can work more efficiently than others and take over key positions." Selling oil barrels on the black market Iran can draw on decades of experience in operating under sanctions. The system extends far beyond individual businessmen and includes a vast network of companies, financial channels and personal connections. Corruption and a lack of transparency are widely regarded as structural problems within Iran's political and economic system. Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index 2025 gave Iran a score of 23 out of 100 and ranked it 153rd out of 182 countries, indicating a very high perceived level of public-sector corruption. Zanjani reportedly controlled a business empire of around 60 companies, including entities in Malaysia, Tajikistan, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates. Many of these firms were later sanctioned by the United States. Through this network, Zanjani began selling billions of barrels of Iranian oil on the black market during the presidency of Mahmoud Ahmadinejad , while also importing a wide range of goods, including aircraft, into Iran. Is Iran set to become an economic outcast? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In 2016, however, he became entangled in Iran's internal power struggles. Authorities accused him of failing to return around $2.6 billion (€2.24 billion) in oil revenues to the Iranian state. After a highly publicized trial in one of the country's biggest corruption cases, he was sentenced to death. For years, he disputed claims over the missing funds and negotiated with Iranian authorities. US gains insight into sanctions evasion routes A key link in this network was Turkish-Iranian businessman Reza Zarrab. He was arrested in the United States in 2016 while on vacation and accused of money laundering and violating US sanctions on Iran. Zarrab had built an extensive network in Turkey and possessed detailed knowledge of the financial and trading mechanisms Iran used to bypass sanctions. Cases such as his gave US authorities valuable insight into how Iranian sanctions evasion networks operate, allowing Washington to target them more effectively. Zarrab later cooperated with US investigators and was released from custody. According to reports, he now lives in the United States under a new identity. "People like Zarrab or Zanjani are cultivated within the system and maintain connections to different centers of power," France-based economist Jamshid Assadi told DW. Can the US 'asphyxiate' Iran without taking on China? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video According to reports, Zanjani's rise began some 30 years ago during his military service, when he worked as a driver for the governor of Iran's central bank. The position is said to have opened doors to influential circles and provided him with key business contacts. How many billions of dollars flowed through his network and companies, and how much he personally earned from those activities, remains unclear. In February 2024, Iranian media reported that assets linked to Zanjani had been repatriated from abroad. His wealth, they said, had grown beyond the value of his outstanding liabilities. In 2025, he was released from prison and quickly returned to the business world. Through one of his companies, he signed a multibillion-dollar contract with Iran's state railway operator. At the same time, Zanjani has sought to reinvent himself. In an open letter to US business magnate Elon Musk, he offered his company as a bridge for economic cooperation between Iran and the United States. He now presents himself as an entrepreneur, mediator and advocate of dialogue. After the United States placed Zanjani back on its sanctions list in January 2026, Washington expanded its measures in July to target a broader network of companies and business associates linked to him. Just one day before the new sanctions were announced, Zanjani opened a cafe and pastry shop in western Tehran and attended a celebratory launch event. The business was shut down by authorities the following day. Allies to adversaries: US-Iran relations over the decades To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Can the US cripple Iran's shadow networks? The key question, however, is whether the latest US measures can truly reach the networks underpinning Iran's shadow economy. According to Assadi, many of the traditional sanctions evasion routes are now well known and increasingly difficult for Tehran to use. The United States has warned numerous countries that their companies, banks and private-sector actors could face penalties if they help Iran bypass restrictions. At the same time, Iran has spent decades adapting to economic pressure and finding new ways around it. Whether Washington's latest sanctions will significantly weaken those networks remains uncertain. But the return of Babak Zanjani suggests Tehran is once again turning to the businessmen who helped it weather previous periods of economic isolation. This article was originally written in German. Kristin Johnson Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Monica Taylor of Media Slip Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Emmanuel Lightbourn Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Emmanuel Lightbourn I n 1989, The Washington City Paper commissioned Lloyd Wolf to photograph the men in the Pilot Substance Abuse Program [PSAP] at Lorton Prison. Those photos are currently on display at the Workhouse Arts Center through Nov. 7. They were intended to accompany an article about the program. “The journalist was Jon Cohen, and he came in to write about the Pilot Substance Abuse Program and wasn’t welcomed by the men enrolled in the program. Obviously, they’re going through a hard time. There’s not a lot of motivation to tell the story,” said Sarah Berry, curator for the exhibition “TRANSFORMATIONS: Documenting the Pilot Substance Abuse Program at Lorton Reformatory, 1989–1991.” She said he returned home discouraged but determined. Instead of giving up, he came back and said, “All right, go ahead and write your story. I’ll join the program and teach you how to tell it.” Kristin Johnson Wolf took a different approach. He built trust slowly. Early on, he was frequently made fun of, but PSAP was a year-long program. He started bringing small prints of his photos to the men involved. He viewed the photos as an exchange so he was not just taking their image from them. He sat in on many of their meetings and activities. He got to know them, and they got to know him. “I found that you can’t just walk in, I mean, you know, you barge in, you get something, but you don’t get depth. Since I had all the time in the world, it helped,” said Wolf. “I learned a lot from a man who ran the program, Dr. Ormond, that with well-run programs, people can get better. And I watched that happen.” Lloyd Wolf stands with some of the photos he took of the members of the Pilot Substance Abuse Program. Kristin Johnson For Wolf, the year had a significant impact. In addition to photographing PSAP at Lorton, he went to Auschwitz on a “March for the Living.” These annual events, which still take place, began in 1988. Wolf explained that this was the first program that allowed Jews to head into the Nazi death camps in large numbers. Wolf went in 1990. Wolf’s father escaped from Nazi Germany in the 1930s, and he met some of his cousins during his trip. When he returned, he found that “Lorton looked a little bit like Auschwitz.” There were no gas chambers, and the purpose was different from the death camps, but mentally Wolf was making the connection, which left him emotional. Monica Taylor of Media Slip Wolf remembered Lorton as one of the most masculine places in the world. When the program began, he described participants as street-tough and swearing. He noticed something different on his return from Poland. Some men had a grievance against a prison official, and they were formally addressing it in a letter. “I got teary with them, and they were teasing me. You know, they knew me, and they said, ‘You know, photographer got a shine on.’ My face was wet. One of the Muslim guys saw that I was emotional, and we sat in a stairwell. His name is Isaac,” said Wolf, who added they sat there until he calmed down. “It took a lot of those kinds of interchanges to do this.” Emmanuel Lightbourn Wolf was referring to the portraits displayed throughout the exhibition, including one hanging several yards away that he pointed out: an image of a man standing in a hallway, likely the photograph he captured of Isaac during that encounter. Wolf’s work is marked by a deep sense of humanity, revealing a rare ability to capture both a subject’s resilience and vulnerability in a single frame. Meanwhile, Cohen helped cultivate a rich collection of essays, prose and poetry from participants, providing a literary complement to the exhibition’s visual storytelling. Berry has wanted to tell this piece of the prison’s 91-year history for a while. She found marking 25 years since the prison closed to be the perfect time. The exhibition also aligns well with the gallery’s mission to show fine art. “It’s an odd feeling because I’m getting older and time compresses,” said Wolf, who is 74. “In my mind this was not that long ago, but it was almost half a lifetime ago.” Everyone graduated, and Wolf took a photo at their graduation. Recidivism was low, but they had been handpicked, and their families also received counseling to improve their odds. In the years since the article was published, Wolf has run into PSAP graduates from time to time. The last time was about 10 years ago. “He didn’t want to give himself away, and he goes, ‘You know a Dr. Ormond?’” said Wolf. “I don’t remember his name at the moment, but he’d become a laborer. He was doing concrete work or rebar work. He’d made a life for himself and stayed, okay.” As visitors move through the gallery, the photographs serve as more than a record of a prison program from decades past. They capture moments of growth, vulnerability and human connection that continued long after the cameras were put away. For Wolf, seeing the images displayed 35 years later is a reminder that the men of PSAP were more than inmates. They were people striving to change their lives. The occasional graduate he has encountered over the years, including one who built a career and stayed out of prison, stands as a testament to the hope that fueled the program and the enduring power of the stories preserved in both words and photographs. https://www.dw.com/en/bulgaria-highway-p.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PHiM Prefer DW on Google Local media images showed cars and trucks scattered across six lanes of highway, with many vehicles mangled, overturned or forced off the road Image: BGNES Advertisement At least 12 people have been killed and dozens more injured in a series of crashes on both sides of a highway in Bulgaria on Tuesday, Bulgarian authorities said. According to the interior ministry, a bus and truck collided, leading to a pileup on the side of the A1 highway near the southeastern city of Yambol. Weather conditions believed to be a factor Speaking to reporters at the site, ministry's general secretary Ministry Lyubomir Nikolov said that fog was likely the cause of the accident. The regional governor of Yambol Georgi Chalakov, said an estimated 50 cars and trucks were involved in the accident. Health Minister Katya Ivkova said 10 people “died on the spot” and two others died while being transported to a hospital. She said 46 people were also injured and transported to medical facilities. Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who was welcoming European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen , cleared his schedule for later Tuesday. Von der Leyen said she would cut her ​visit short. Focus on rescue operations Police, firefighters and paramedics were dispatched to the scene on the A1 highway connecting the capital Sofia to the Black Sea city of Burgas. Aircrafts carrying medical teams have been dispatched to the scene Image: BGNES Chief Inspector ⁠Todor Mishinev from the Yambol Regional Directorate of the Ministry of Internal Affairs ⁠told Nova TV that people were still trapped in their cars at the time of speaking. "Right now, the priority is rescue operations. Once they are completed, the procedural and investigative actions will be carried out," he said. The injured were being taken to hospitals in nearby cities, while authorities dispatched two aircraft carrying medical teams and stretcher equipment. Bulgaria saw 71 road fatalities per million inhabitants in 2025, the highest rate in the European Union, according to European Commission figures. For orientation, EU average is 43 per million. Victims say reckless driving, neglected road infrastructure and an inefficient justice system contribute to the country's high number of fatal traffic accidents.
